To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) trade union confederational governance matters; (b) worker involvement in contract bargaining ratification is a confederational governance mechanism that has significant wage-dampening effects; (c) collective bargaining centralization and coordination are also wage-dampening mechanisms; (d) the effects of worker involvement and collective bargaining coordination are mutually reinforcing; and (e) the wage-dampening mechanism of worker involvement is more powerful than the wage-dampenning effects of bargaining centralization and

the wage-setting process is more likely to be wage-moderating in countries where trade union confederational leaders have the support of a large majority of their affiliates and where they can rely on a high degree of worker involvement in the contract ratification process.

(a) the organizational characteristics of the trade unions, and in particular their involvement in contract ratifications, are significant determinants of wage dynamics; and (b) collective bargaining coordination magnifies the wage-dampening effects of contract ratification.
